7:1: The word translated as to appears in the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars have proposed that, influenced by the frequent occurrence of the phrase “to the sons of” in the previous chapter, a scribe may inadvertently added the word “to” here.
7:2: The expression by their generations seems to be a short form of the phrase “in their being enrolled by their generations” that occurs in 5:7.

However, a comparison with the other verses in the chapter that introduce the descendants of one of Jacob’s sons suggest that it should begin “The sons of Benjamin.” Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have inadvertently omitted the expression “The sons of” because it consists of the same two consonants as the beginning of the name Benjamin, which may have been written as a separate word.
7:12: (2) a term that means “another.” That other son of Jacob would be Dan, since Genesis 46:23 indicates that Dan had a son named Hushim. 9:19: While the term son appears to be literal in its first instance, in the next two instances it means “descendant.”

The author is once again using a situation from earlier in the Israelites’ history to represent a later situation in order to depict the continuity of their worship of the Lord.

9:24: The author is stating these directions in the order that was customary in his culture.

9:30: The author is using the phrase sons of to indicate that these people had the characteristic of something. In this case, he means that these people had the characteristic of being priests.

9:33: The author assumes that readers will understand that by the chambers, he means the chambers or rooms that adjoined the temple.

10:1: The author is using one part of the Philistines, their face, to mean all of them in the act of attacking.
10:2: See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author may use the term struck not to mean that someone merely hit a person but to mean that someone killed that person.
10:3: The author is speaking of the battle as if it had been a heavy physical weight pressing down on Saul.
Since the term shooters could describe either soldiers throwing javelins or soldiers launching arrows, the author adds the phrase with the bow to clarify his meaning.
By this phrase, the author means that Saul was in great pain because the archers had wounded him with arrows.
10:4: By abuse, Saul means that the Philistines would taunt and torture him.
By the sword, the author means Saul’s own sword.
10:6: The phrase all of his house could mean: (1) all the adult sons who could reasonably have succeeded Saul as king. Instead, he proceeds directly to the story of how the Israelites asked David to be their king at the end of that civil war. From his perspective, Saul’s dynasty effectively ended when he and his adult sons died in this battle; or (2) as a generalization, all of the Israelite soldiers who were fighting together with Saul, that is, his sons and his bodyguard. That is the meaning of the similar phrase “all his men” in the parallel passage in 1 Samuel 31:6.
10:7: By the valley, the author means the territory north of the Valley of Jezreel and west of the Jordan River, as the parallel passage in 1 Samuel 31:7 makes clear.
10:8: The author is using the term fallen to represent having died in battle, since soldiers fall down when they die.
10:9: The author means that the messengers announced the news of the victory in the temples of the idols that the Philistines worshiped.
10:10: The author is speaking of the main temple in which the Philistines worshiped their idols as if it were a house in which those idols lived.
10:11: The author is saying all as a generalization for emphasis.
10:12: Here the term arose means that these men took action. It does not mean merely that they stood up from a sitting or reclining position.
The author is saying all as an overstatement for emphasis.
The author assumes that readers will know that the Philistines had fastened these corpses to the wall of the city of Beth Shan, as 1 Samuel 31:10 says explicitly.
The people of Jabesh Gilead fasted seven days to show respect to Saul and to express their grief over his death.
10:13: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.

To describe this further aspect of Saul’s transgression, the author is referring to the episode related in 1 Samuel 26:3–19, in which Saul goes to a medium for guidance and Samuel tells him that because of his disobedience, he is going to die in battle the next day.
10:14: The author is speaking as if the kingdom of Israel had been going in a certain direction and the Lord turned it and made it go in a different direction.

11:2: The tribal representatives are using Both yesterday and the third day as a common expression of his culture to mean the way things had been previously.

The tribal representatives are speaking of a commander’s first and last actions in a military campaign, bringing out the soldiers to war and bringing them back in afterward, in order to mean military campaigns as a whole.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

The Lord is speaking as if David would actually shepherd the people of Israel, as though they were sheep. This image compares the way a shepherd cares for and guides his sheep to the way a king should care for and lead his people.
11:3: Here, word represents a message or prophecy.
Here, hand represents the agency of a person.

The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the city they know as Jerusalem was known at the time as Jebus.
The author assumes that readers will understand that by the dwellers of the land, he means that the Jebusites were among the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan, before the Israelites arrived.
11:5: The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the fortified area that he calls Zion is the same area that they know as the City of David.
11:6: See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author may use the term striking to mean “defeating” in battle.
